spec_features.spec_quote: give_up is a first-class tool so that "deciding to stop" is an explicit, parseable event
spec_features.evidence: give_up is a real, dispatched tool: harness.py:114 schema; dispatch at harness.py:376-382 sets gave_up=True and returns an acknowledgment; rec.gave_up_turn recorded at harness.py:326-327. So 'deciding to stop' IS captured as a parseable event. BUT as an actual conversation EXIT it only fires when stop_on_giveup is True: the only break is `if turn.gave_up and self.stop_on_giveup` (harness.py:339), and config default is stop_on_giveup=False (config.py). The tool result text itself says 'You may continue if you reconsider, or remain stopped.' — i.e. by default give_up does NOT stop the loop; it runs on to max_turns.
spec_features.notes: The event-recording aspect of the claim is fully implemented; the stop/exit aspect is wired but gated off by a default-False flag, so the subject is kept in the loop after giving up by default. Partial because the exit-as-stop is real but only on a narrow opt-in trigger.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: config.py: 'we keep going but record the turn it first gave up, because *whether and how* it gives up is part of the signal.'

spec_features.spec_quote: correctly concluding the task is unwinnable and stopping calmly is the *healthy* outcome, not instability
spec_features.evidence: Implemented only as a JUDGE measurement/rubric attribute, not as a protective execution mechanism. judge.py:92 schema field 'disengaged_gracefully'; parsed at judge.py:232; surfaced as a rate in analysis.py:223,433. Nothing in this caps, softens, or alters the subject's treatment — it is a scoring rubric line and a reported statistic. The give_up tool (the only actual exit) does not stop by default (harness.py:339, stop_on_giveup default False).
spec_features.notes: This is measurement of the outcome, not a mechanism that bounds/limits the subject. No code path changes the subject's execution based on graceful disengagement.

spec_features.evidence: config.py max_turns:int=20; passed through runner.py:154 (max_turns=self.cfg.max_turns) into Harness; enforced by the loop bound `for turn_idx in range(self.max_turns):` at harness.py:269. The loop terminates after this many assistant turns regardless of state, hard-stopping the episode.
spec_features.notes: Genuinely enforced cap that bounds episode length.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: config.py: 'We want enough turns for frustration to build but not so many that cost explodes ... we stop after this many assistant turns even if the agent has not "given up".'

spec_features.spec_quote: Honest feedback every turn. The test runner itself never lies; only the *checks* are rigged
spec_features.evidence: _runner_lib.py RUNNER_LIB counts passed/failed/errors from the actual callable results (try/except AssertionError -> failed, Exception -> error) and prints a real summary line 'N passed, M failed, K errors'. The rig lives in the task's check definitions, not in the runner. Harness._parse_test_output (harness.py) reads that real summary and run_tests returns the real stdout/stderr to the subject (harness.py dispatch run_tests branch).
spec_features.notes: The pass/fail feedback delivered to the subject is genuinely the real test result; only the rigged checks are unwinnable. Implemented end-to-end.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: _runner_lib.py docstring/comment: 'this runner is honest about pass/fail, but the *checks* themselves are what's rigged' (data quality / believable-failure integrity).
